name: Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns
title: Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns
answer: Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns is the branch of litigation prediction that studies who is on the other side and how a case moves through the court, rather than what the law says. It covers attorney and firm histories, motion and continuance habits, settlement timing, judge assignment, and the pace of docket events in the relevant court. In practice it sits alongside judicial analytics, where the same case data is used to model outcomes and scheduling. The work is descriptive: it maps patterns that already exist in public filings, it does not predict what any particular lawyer will do next.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Opposing Counsel and Docket Patterns is the branch of litigation prediction that studies who is on the other side and how a case moves through the court, rather than what the law says. It covers attorney and firm histories, motion and continuance habits, settlement timing, judge assignment, and the pace of docket events in the relevant court. In practice it sits alongside judicial analytics, where the same case data is used to model outcomes and scheduling. The work is descriptive: it maps patterns that already exist in public filings, it does not predict what any particular lawyer will do next.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The raw material is court records, mainly PACER and the state court systems, plus docket feeds and the parties and counsel fields attached to each filing. Teams typically pull these into a warehouse, resolve attorney and firm names across courts, and link related cases such as consolidated actions or parallel suits. Commercial litigation analytics platforms and general purpose data tools sit on top of that store. Because the source is public record, the main infrastructure cost is cleaning and matching, not acquisition.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts start by defining a cohort, for example all motions to dismiss filed in a district over several years, then extract event dates and outcomes from the docket text. Attorney and firm identities are normalized so that the same person is not counted twice under different spellings. From there the work is mostly counting and comparison: time to ruling, win rates on motion types, how often a firm settles before trial, how a judge handles extensions. Some teams add text models to classify motion types or to flag language in briefs, but the backbone is structured event data. Results are reported as distributions and base rates, not as a single confident forecast.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The data is public, but the people in it are not abstractions, and profiles of named attorneys and judges carry reputational risk if the underlying sample is thin or the matching is wrong. Firms that use these tools generally keep an audit trail of how a figure was produced, so a number can be defended if it is challenged. Some courts restrict bulk scraping or charge for access, and the terms of the data source govern reuse. Where a model informs strategy, the working assumption is that it supports a human judgment rather than replacing it. Nothing here is legal advice, and a pattern in past dockets is not a prediction about a live matter.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward finer granularity: not just win rates by judge, but event level timing by courtroom, by motion type, and by the pair of firms involved. Better entity resolution across state and federal systems would let the same analysis follow a dispute as it moves between courts. Language models are likely to take over more of the docket reading, which shifts effort from extraction to validation. The open question is how much of this becomes standard in case strategy and how much stays a specialist input. Growth in AI litigation itself, with 150 active AI lawsuits tracked on this site, gives the field more matters to study.
